findings.paper_title: PB 2026 09 04 Business Plan - App 2 - Worcestershire Pension Fund - Annual check on contribution rates for admitted bodies
findings.headline: Overall pension fund deteriorated 5 percentage points in one year, driven by rising liability values and market volatility
findings.detail: Worcestershire Pension Fund's overall funding level fell from 127% (31 March 2025) to 122% (31 March 2026). The deterioration is due to rising liability values from higher inflation expectations and lower expected future asset returns, partially offset by asset gains. Recent Middle East geopolitical tensions caused additional market volatility, though asset performance has recovered since 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: A weakening funding position could eventually require the council to increase its pension contributions, though 122% funded remains solid and the fund remains in strong surplus
findings.figures: Whole Fund funding level fell from 127% to 122%; liabilities approximately £4,200m, assets approximately £5,100m
findings.quote: The whole Fund funding level at 31 March 2026 was 122% (in comparison to 127% as at 31 March 2025). Despite volatility in asset and liability values, the funding level increased over the period to December 2025, however recent geo-political tensions have resulted in a deterioration of the funding level in recent months (March 2026 in particular).

findings.paper_title: PB 2026 09 04 Business Plan - App 2 - Worcestershire Pension Fund - Annual check on contribution rates for admitted bodies
findings.headline: Two contractors have fallen below their funding thresholds, but actuaries recommend not changing contribution rates yet
findings.detail: Arete Outdoor Centre (420) and Kidderminster District Youth Trust (472) have seen their likelihood of success fall to 65%, below the 70% threshold for Temporary Admission Bodies. The actuaries note these employers warrant consideration for contribution rate reviews under LGPS regulations, but explicitly recommend against reviewing them now due to market volatility and improving funding positions since 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council faces unexpected pension contribution increases, and these threshold breaches could signal future employer contribution rises, though they are being deferred pending stabilization
findings.figures: 65% likelihood of success for both employers; 70% is the minimum threshold for TABs
findings.quote: The likelihood of full funding for the two TABs paying low, but non-zero, contribution rates has fallen below the required 70% threshold. The Fund should therefore consider whether a review of contribution rates is appropriate for these employers. However, for the reasons set out above, my advice is that a review is not required at this stage.

findings.paper_title: 7 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26- Cabinet final
findings.headline: Other Long-Term Liabilities exceeded both authorised and operational limits due to IFRS 16 restatement
findings.detail: Other long-term liabilities of £129.4m breached both the authorised limit (£126.5m) and operational boundary (£126.5m). The Council describes this as a technical breach arising from a reassessment of existing obligations under IFRS 16, not new debt. However, any breach of established limits is a control and governance issue.
findings.matters: While the breach is stated to be technical rather than substantive, it represents a control failure against policy limits. Any limit breach raises questions about oversight and whether other limits are being similarly strained.
findings.figures: £129.4m actual vs £126.5m limit; £2.9m overage
findings.quote: Other long-term liabilities are shown as above both the authorised limit and the operational boundary due to a paper reassessment under IFRS 16. This is a technical breach – the council has not taken on additional debt in respect of other long-term liabilities.

findings.paper_title: 7 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26- Cabinet final
findings.headline: Cash position declined by £15.8m to £15.7m, compressed by borrowing demand and DSG deficit
findings.detail: Cash and cash equivalents fell from £31.5m to £15.7m over the year (a 50% reduction). The Council offset this by using internal borrowing (£27.7m) to fund the gap between its underlying borrowing need and external borrowing taken. This combination—declining cash plus heavy reliance on reserves—indicates constrained liquidity.
findings.matters: Low cash reserves (£15.7m against total debt of £725.2m) limit the Council's ability to absorb shocks or delay borrowing, and increase dependence on maintaining access to credit markets.
findings.figures: Cash fall from £31.5m to £15.7m (£15.8m reduction); internal borrowing £27.7m
findings.quote: The difference between the underlying need to borrow (excluding PFI) and external borrowing was £27.7 million, which was financed temporarily by 'internal borrowing' i.e. the use of reserves and working capital

findings.paper_title: 7 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26- Cabinet final
findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £118.1m in one year, with underlying need to borrow up £21.9m
findings.detail: Total external borrowing rose from £607.1m to £725.2m (a net increase of £118.1m, or 18.4%). Simultaneously, the underlying Capital Financing Requirement increased from £731.0m to £752.9m. The Council covered £27.7m of this need through internal borrowing (drawing on reserves and cash), rather than accessing external markets.
findings.matters: A £118.1m increase in one year substantially raises the Council's debt servicing obligations and revenue cost. Use of internal borrowing to cover part of the gap signals tightening cash position and reduced financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £118.1m net borrowing increase; total external debt £725.2m; underlying need £752.9m; internal borrowing £27.7m
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council held £725.2 million of loans, which was a net increase of £118.1 million from 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: 7 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26- Cabinet final
findings.headline: £180.8m Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is driving borrowing strategy and depleting financial resilience
findings.detail: The High Need Deficit in schools funding reached £180.8m by March 2026, consuming the Council's resource base. This structural deficit is the core reason for both the increased borrowing requirement and the deliberate choice to use short-term rather than long-term debt. Even if the expected £162m grant arrives, a gap of approximately £18.8m remains unfunded.
findings.matters: A £180.8m cumulative deficit representing a fundamental structural problem signals chronic underfunding in schools. Until government support arrives, this deficit must be financed from Council resources, reducing reserves and increasing leverage; any delay in the grant creates immediate liquidity and budget pressure.
findings.figures: £180.8m DSG deficit reserve; £162m expected High Needs Stability Grant; ~£18.8m residual gap
findings.quote: due to the current £180.8 million DSG deficit reserve is impacting the resource-base of the balance sheet, as of 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 7 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26- Cabinet final
findings.headline: Maturity structure breach: 31.1% of debt matures within one year, exceeding the 0-25% policy upper limit
findings.detail: The Council held £225.2m (31.1% of £725.2m total borrowing) maturing within 12 months, breaching its upper limit of 0-25%. Officers made this choice deliberately, opting for short-term borrowing rather than longer-term loans to protect the revenue budget while interest rates remained high. The strategy assumes receipt of a £162m High Needs Stability Grant before end of 2026/27, after which debt can be refinanced or repaid.
findings.matters: Short-term debt creates refinancing risk: if the expected grant is delayed or reduced, or if interest rates rise further when £225.2m comes due for renewal, the Council faces material cost increases or liquidity pressure.
findings.figures: £225.2m maturing in 1 year (31.1% of £725.2m total); upper policy limit 0-25%
findings.quote: Officers has chosen to utilise short-term borrowing rather than longer term borrowing to protect the revenue budget and understanding that the council is to receive a High Needs Stability Grant of c£162m before the end of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 07 21 AG Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Six audits across control and governance areas returned 'unsatisfactory' or 'needs improvement' ratings
findings.detail: Out of 39 audit pieces of work, 2 were unsatisfactory and 4 were 'needs improvement'. Areas flagged include business continuity planning, performance data tracking, contracts management (tendering process not always followed), declaration of interests not captured, s106 monies control, and data retention/handling. All recommendations were accepted by management but implementation remains outstanding for 17 of 65 actions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether controls are reliable. Governance and compliance failures in procurement, interest declarations, and contracts create fraud risk and suggest management cannot be relied on to enforce internal controls consistently.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 07 21 AG Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Financial resilience concern: council was recently bordering between 'needs improvement' and 'satisfactory', and savings plan required to balance 2025-26
findings.detail: The auditor notes that 'over the past twelve months...the assurance level was bordering between ''needs improvement' and 'satisfactory' assurance.' A robust savings plan was agreed for 2025-26 to assist with balancing the council's finances, monitored throughout the year. The report identifies 'on going financial pressures for coming years' as a significant risk.
findings.matters: Council was recently in weaker financial health than the current 'satisfactory' rating suggests, requiring active intervention (savings plan) to balance the budget. Ongoing pressures indicate the improvement may not be durable.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 07 21 AG Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: High Needs Deficit remains a 'significant' financial sustainability risk despite 90% government support
findings.detail: The council faces structural funding gaps in demand-led services, particularly High Needs. Central Government offers only 90% support dependent on application, while the council is mandated to provide the service. The report states funding 'remains short of covering the actual incurred expense' and identifies this as a continuing 'significant' risk to financial sustainability, with ongoing financial pressures expected in coming years.
findings.matters: A structural gap between statutory service demand and available funding creates borrowing pressure and raises questions about medium-term solvency. The council cannot refuse the service but cannot cover its cost.
findings.figures: Central Government support capped at 90% dependent on application; mandate to provide service with shortfall funding
findings.quote: Although Central Government is offering to provide 90% support depending on application, to offset the High Needs Deficit, this continues to be a 'significant' risk to the Council regarding financial sustainability. The Council is mandated to provide this on demand service, but the ongoing funding remains short of covering the actual incurred expense.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Budget - Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council must take unprecedented short-term borrowing to cover underfunded SEND High Needs until March 2028
findings.detail: The Government has not funded SEND High Needs adequately through the Dedicated Schools Grant, forcing Worcestershire into additional short-term borrowing of £127.6m in 2026/27, rising to £160.7m in 2027/28. The council is losing approximately £7.5m annually in treasury management income as a result. The Government will not take responsibility for cumulative deficits until March 2028, leaving the council to bridge the gap with interest-bearing debt—effectively providing an interest-free loan to the Department for Education. The CFO explicitly states this would have prevented them meeting balanced budget requirements in 2025/26 without this shortfall.
findings.matters: This forces the council into substantial short-term borrowing that must be refinanced multiple times before 2028, creating cumulative interest costs and cash-flow volatility. The lack of clarity on how government will manage historic deficits after March 2028 leaves the council's medium-term sustainability uncertain.
findings.figures: £7.5m annual treasury income loss; £93.6m DSG borrowing 2025/26; £127.6m in 2026/27; £160.7m in 2027/28; debt including DSG projected to reach £1,248.3m by March 2028
findings.quote: This means that the cumulative impact is growing exponentially and the effect on sustainability is ever increasing, due to lost interest income and higher borrowing costs, with councils effectively providing an interest-free loan to the Department for Education.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of revenue forecast to rise in 2027/28 after initial decline
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (borrowing interest and MRP) to net revenue stream is forecast to decline from 7.04% (2025/26) to 6.80% (2026/27), but then rise to 6.98% in 2027/28. This reflects the growing debt burden from both capital expenditure and DSG cashflowing. The 2027/28 increase occurs just as the DSG deficit pressure reaches its peak.
findings.matters: A rising ratio of financing costs to revenue shows an increasing share of the council's income committed to debt service, constraining flexibility for service spending. The uptick in 2027/28 coincides with maximum DSG pressure and capital expenditure commitments.
findings.quote: The estimates of financing costs include current commitments and the proposals in this budget report. [Table 6 showing Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates remain elevated despite base rate cuts; 50-year loans peaked at 6.14%
findings.detail: Despite the Bank of England reducing base rate from 4.50% to 3.75% during 2025, Public Works Loan Board rates for longer-term borrowing have remained stubbornly high. The 50-year rate peaked at 6.14% and is forecast to remain above 5% through the forecast period. This constrains the council's borrowing options, particularly for long-term funding.
findings.matters: A borrowing council facing multiple demands (capital programme, DSG deficit, maturing debt) benefits from falling rates. Persistent elevation in PWLB rates raises the cost of meeting those demands, especially for the 25+ year maturities often used in local authority borrowing.
findings.figures: 50-year PWLB rate: 5.63% (1 April 2025) to 5.71% (31 December 2025); High: 6.14%; forecast for 2026/27: 5.81%
findings.quote: Despite the general downward trend in inflation and BoE base rates, PWLB rates have remained high, with 25 and 50-year loans peaking at around 6%

findings.headline: Treasury investments fell 46% in nine months; external debt rose £72 million in same period
findings.detail: Cash reserves held as treasury investments fell from £57.5 million (31 March 2025) to £31.0 million (30 December 2025). findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Prudential borrowing limit breached when DSG is included, forecast to persist through 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's gross debt will exceed the prudential control limit (the Capital Financing Requirement) in 2027/28 and 2028/29 when DSG-related borrowing is included. findings.matters: Prudential borrowing limits exist to prevent excessive debt accumulation. A breach signals the council is operating outside normal borrowing constraints, even if justified by government policy. This persists for two years.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure and CFR to grow significantly, driven partly by Exceptional Financial Support assumptions
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is forecast to peak at £193.8 million in 2026/27 (up 29% from 2025/26), driving the Capital Financing Requirement to £873.7 million by end of March 2027. Of this growth, £71.9 million is assumed to come from government Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27, with a further £71.0 million assumed in 2027/28. The CFR will continue growing to £996.6 million by March 2028.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this capital growth is self-sustaining or dependent on government support. The EFS assumptions are conditional on government approval and represent significant uncertainty in the borrowing forecast.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: High Needs deficit requires continuous short-term borrowing until March 2028
findings.detail: The council is cashflowing a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) High Needs deficit by taking short-term borrowing. In 2025/26 alone this cost £7.5 million in lost treasury management income. The cumulative deficit is growing exponentially, with the government not taking over responsibility until March 2028. External debt including DSG is forecast to reach £1,248.3 million by March 2029.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council is obliged to borrow to cover a deficit it did not create, and this obligation persists for two more financial years. The cumulative, exponential growth suggests the position worsens each year rather than stabilising.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Three-year settlement creates 2028/29 funding 'cliff edge': large funding floor payments will leave councils 'substantially above their funding target' with unclear solution
findings.detail: The provisional and final settlements provide 3-year certainty but large funding floor payments will leave many authorities (including Worcestershire) substantially above funding target in 2028/29. The government has not yet clarified how this 'cliff edge' will be handled in the next multi-year settlement, creating ongoing uncertainty. Wychavon District Council will receive £5.5 million of income protection in 2028/29; Worcestershire gets none.
findings.matters: Unresolved funding cliff edge beyond the MTFP creates material downside risk to forward projections and could force a second structural deficit if not managed carefully.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power increases: 2026/27 £578m, 2027/28 £601.7m, 2028/29 £626.6m; Wychavon income protection 2028/29 £5.5m; Worcestershire income protection over 3 years £0m
findings.quote: Large funding floor payments, combined with the continued Recovery Grant, will leave a large number of authorities substantially above their funding target in 2028/29. It is not clear how this funding "cliff edge" will be handled going into the next multi-year settlement (although it was referenced in the local government minister's statement). It creates ongoing uncertainty, and unfairness.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Exceptional Council Tax flexibility (4%) exhausted and insufficient; only 7 councils nationally granted this permission
findings.detail: Worcestershire is one of only 7 councils in England granted exceptional council tax flexibility above the 4.99% referendum limit (others: Bournemouth, Trafford, Windsor & Maidenhead, Warrington, Shropshire, North Somerset). The 4% additional flexibility is worth £14.4 million per year or £43.2 million over the MTFP. This is presented as 'critical to the council's current and future financial sustainability' but remains insufficient to close the gap.
findings.matters: The fact that Worcestershire has exhausted exceptional council tax flexibilities available only to 7 councils signals government recognition of structural distress, and narrows future income-raising options.
findings.figures: £14.4 million per year from 4% flexibility; £43.2 million over MTFP period; 8.98% total increase (6.98% + 2% ASC precept)
findings.quote: For Worcestershire, at the maximum, this is worth an additional £14.4 million per year and £43.2 million over the MTFP Period.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Children's Social Care demand accelerating: external placements +6% in 12 months, Agency Residential unit costs rising £590/week
findings.detail: Looked After Children external placements increased from 651 to 690 year-on-year by December 2025. Agency Residential placements at 180 children (up from 162), with weekly costs rising from £6,563 to £7,153 per week. Two new Secure placements at £18,391/week. The council's placement growth rate (2%) combined with cost inflation (5.5% to 7%+) is driving £6.5 million overspend in Children's despite placement prevention efforts.
findings.matters: Rising LAC placement demand coupled with market-driven cost inflation creates a cost pressure that cannot be managed by internal controls. It signals either sufficiency of the prevention budget or deeper systemic pressures in family support.
findings.figures: External placements: 651 (Dec 2024) to 690 (Dec 2025), +6%; Agency Residential: 180 children; cost rise £590/week (£6,563 to £7,153); Secure placements: 2 new at £18,391/week; forecast overspend £6.5 million
findings.quote: At the end of December, the numbers of children placed in Agency Residential had increased to 180 from 162 at the end of March and average unit costs increased from £6,563/week to £7,153/week in December.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Risk reserves projected to fall to £17 million by March 2027, described as 'not a prudent level' to cover overspend risk
findings.detail: Total council reserves (excluding General Fund) are projected to decline from £93.7 million at March 2025 to £45.8 million at March 2027 and £35.5 million by 2029 (62% reduction). Risk reserves specifically drop to £17 million by March 2027. The Section 151 Officer assessment identifies this as insufficient to cover potential overspends, savings delivery delays, or other materialised risks.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves below prudent levels removes the council's buffer against any adverse variance, making it vulnerable to budget shocks and potentially forcing mid-year savings notices or further government intervention.
findings.figures: Total reserves March 2025: £93.7 million; March 2027: £45.8 million; March 2029: £35.5 million (62% decline); Risk reserves March 2027: £17 million; General Fund 4% of net spend (£19.2 million)
findings.quote: the value of the Risk Reserves drops to £17 million at the end of 2026/27 which is not a prudent level of reserves remaining to cover risks of overspends, delay in delivery of savings or other risks that may materialise.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: 2025/26 outturn forecast shows £13.3 million service overspend covered by £17.2 million reserves and £33.6 million one-off EFS
findings.detail: Adults Services overspending by £12.4 million (placement growth of 183 in 9 months, unit cost inflation up to 15.5% for Physical Disability), Children's overspending by £10.1 million (external placements +6%, Agency Residential costs rising from £6,563 to £7,153 per week). The council is covering this with non-renewable reserves and exceptional funding, indicating the underlying budget is unsustainable.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years (2024/25 and 2025/26) of significant social care overspends covered by one-off mitigations demonstrate the council cannot live within its budget envelope. This is a leading indicator of structural insolvency.
findings.figures: £13.3 million service overspend 2025/26; £12.4 million Adults overspend; £10.1 million Children's overspend; 183 net new Adult placements in 9 months; Physical Disability Residential inflation 15.5%; Agency Residential weekly cost increase £6,563 to £7,153
findings.quote: Services are overspending by £13.3 million, partially offset by savings of £11.1 million on corporate items including a reduction in borrowing and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) and a reduction in expected utilisation of the corporate contingency.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Accumulated High Needs SEND deficit of £194.1 million with 10% unfunded liability (£43.7 million) by 2028
findings.detail: Worcestershire carried a cumulative High Needs deficit of £98.2 million into 2025/26 and is forecast to close at £194.1 million. While the government will fund 90% via a High Needs Stability Grant (£174 million), the council must build reserves for the remaining 10% (£43.7 million by 31 March 2028). The council has cash-flowed approximately £200 million to fund this deficit to date and may need to borrow shortly if timings worsen.
findings.matters: A £194 million DSG deficit is exceptional and creates immediate borrowing obligations. The 10% unfunded gap could force material cuts to SEND services or further budget amendments if reserve-building proves unachievable.
findings.figures: £194.1 million accumulated deficit forecast end 2025/26; £174 million government support (90%); £43.7 million unfunded 10% liability; £200 million cash flowed to date; £437 million projected deficit by March 2028
findings.quote: Worcestershire carried a cumulative High Needs deficit of £98.2 million into 2025/26 and is forecast to close the year with an accumulated deficit of £194.1 million. This has a significant impact on our Treasury Management activities, as at March 2026, Worcestershire will have cash flowed c£200 million to fund this deficit.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: £59.933 million unfunded budget gap requires government capitalisation directive approval to set a balanced budget
findings.detail: After approved savings of £8.975 million and an 8.98% council tax increase (including 4% exceptional flexibility), the council still faces a remaining gap of £59.933 million for 2026/27. The council has received provisional approval from MHCLG on 23 February 2026 for a capitalisation directive covering this full amount, without which the Section 151 officer would be forced to issue a Section 114 notice (statutory insolvency warning).
findings.matters: A council relying on capitalisation directives to balance operating budgets signals structural financial failure and becomes a credit risk, as borrowing must be repaid from revenue over 20 years at estimated cost of £1.9 million annually per £20 million borrowed.
findings.figures: £59.933 million gap; £8.975 million approved savings; 8.98% council tax increase (6.98% + 2% ASC precept); capitalisation directive at full £59.933 million
findings.quote: Without the use of EFS, the Council will not be able to balance the 2026/27 budget. This situation will force the Section 151 officer to use his statutory powers and issue a section 114 notice in the absence of further measures or robust and deliverable recurrent savings.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition costs potentially exceeding £20 million must be funded by all seven authorities with no national funding, adding pressure during peak financial constraint
findings.detail: Worcestershire is moving toward a single unitary authority (vesting April 2028) following LGR proposals submitted by the seven local authorities in November 2025. Experience from other council mergers suggests transition costs could exceed £20 million. Government has explicitly stated there will be no national funding for these costs, requiring all seven authorities to jointly fund and manage them. The S151 Officer notes this 'will remain a risk going into 2026/27 that will need to be carefully monitored' and that 'all 7 councils in the area will need to work together effectively to jointly contribute and manage the required transition costs as a system.'
findings.matters: Unfunded transition costs of this scale, to be borne during a period of peak financial stress and in a period when the council cannot balance its budget, represent a significant contingent liability and source of additional financial pressure during the critical 2026-28 period.
findings.figures: Transition costs potentially exceeding £20 million; to be funded collectively by 7 authorities; no national funding available; LGR vesting date April 2028
findings.quote: Experience from other councils who have moved from a two-tier system suggests that transition costs could be in excess of £20 million. This is expected to be funded by all 7 local authorities in the area.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Chronic overspends in Children's and Adult Social Care placements show worsening pattern despite management action: £6.2m (2024/25) following £19.1m underlying deficit (2023/24)
findings.detail: The council experiences persistent and growing demand-led overspends in social care. The 2024/25 net overspend was £6.2 million. Before one-off mitigations, 2023/24 showed £19.1 million overspend and 2022/23 showed £22 million. The paper states these pressures 'continue to face relentless demand and cost pressures in both Children's Social Care and Adult Social Care placements which have been reported in our regular financial monitoring reports...over the last few years.' The S151 Officer notes the council's 'over-reliance on the use of reserves and one-off mitigations' and judges that the 'Council's ability to reduce recurrent spend, deliver recurrent savings' is challenged.
findings.matters: A multi-year pattern of unmanaged social care demand growth, masked by one-off reserves and government grants, indicates structural cost pressures the council cannot control, making long-term financial sustainability dependent on service redesign or demand reduction the council has not yet achieved.
findings.figures: 2024/25 net overspend £6.2m; 2023/24 net overspend £19.1m (before mitigations); 2022/23 overspend £22m (before mitigations including £3m one-off social care grant)
findings.quote: The Council's budget for 2025/26 continues to face relentless demand and cost pressures in both Children's Social Care and Adult Social Care placements which have been reported in our regular financial monitoring reports to Cabinet and through to Scrutiny Committees over the last few years.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: External auditor identified significant weaknesses in financial sustainability and issued two formal key recommendations
findings.detail: The auditor's Annual Report (November 2025) confirms 'significant weaknesses in arrangements to ensure the council manages risk to around its financial sustainability.' Two formal Key Recommendations were issued: (KR1) work at pace to reduce EFS reliance and agree a reserves replenishment plan; (KR2) urgently implement savings and transformation at scale with monitoring and mitigation plans for slippages. These formal recommendations indicate independent assessment of systemic control failures.
findings.matters: Independent auditor confirmation of significant weaknesses in financial sustainability is a red flag for credit risk; formal recommendations indicate the auditor does not view current management actions as adequate.
findings.figures: Two formal Key Recommendations issued
findings.quote: The conclusions from the External Auditor are contained within Auditor's Annual Report 2024/25 published in November 2025 which confirms there are significant weaknesses in arrangements to ensure the council manages risk to around its financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund reserves are only 3.1% of operating budget, below the recommended 5%, with CIPFA rating reserve sustainability as 'higher risk'
findings.detail: The council maintains a General Fund balance of £19.2 million, unchanged from 2025/26, which represents only 3.1% of the proposed £619.9 million operating budget. The S151 Officer notes this 'ideally this should be nearer to 5%'. The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index identifies the council's reserve sustainability measure as 'higher risk' and notes reserves are lower than average relative to nearest neighbours and other unitary authorities. This leaves minimal buffer for unexpected demands.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves below recommended levels, combined with an independent 'higher risk' rating, signal limited capacity to absorb service demand shocks or respond to unforeseen events without triggering further EFS requests.
findings.figures: £19.2 million General Fund balance = 3.1% of £619.9 million budget (target ~5%); equivalent to one to two weeks of net expenditure
findings.quote: This is equivalent to 3.1% of the proposed operating budget of £619.9 million for 2026/27, ideally this should be nearer to 5%. This equates to between one and two weeks of net expenditure.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Only £8.945 million in planned recurrent savings for 2026/27, described by the S151 Officer as 'nowhere near enough' for an organisation of this size
findings.detail: The council has identified just £8.945 million in savings for 2026/27. The Chief Financial Officer explicitly states this is inadequate: 'as £8.945 million is nowhere near enough for an organisation of this size, transformation is the only viable route to deliver savings at the scale and speed required.' This follows a pattern: £12.5 million in 2025/26 and £8.9 million in 2026/27. The council is working with PwC on a transformation plan to close the gap, but delivery is uncertain against mounting LGR implementation commitments.
findings.matters: Acknowledged insufficiency of planned recurrent savings means the budget gap remains unresolved; reliance on 'transformation' (not yet specified) and one-off central government support rather than structural cost control.
findings.figures: £8.945 million planned savings for 2026/27; £12.5 million in 2025/26; £19.1 million overspend before mitigations in 2023/24
findings.quote: as £8.945 million is nowhere near enough for an organisation of this size, and the nature of the challenges faced by the council, transformation is the only viable route to deliver savings at the scale and speed required

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: 2025/26 forecast position is already £2.2 million worse than budgeted, requiring £17.2 million reserves drawdown plus £33.6 million EFS
findings.detail: At Q3 2025/26, the council is forecasting a breakeven position only after using £2.2 million more reserves than the budgeted £15 million, plus £33.6 million of Exceptional Financial Support. Services show a £13.3 million overspend, partially offset by £11.1 million in corporate savings (chiefly reduced borrowing costs). This demonstrates inability to deliver even within adjusted forecasts mid-year.
findings.matters: An in-year forecast that slips by £2.2 million in just nine months, requiring emergency central government support to avoid a Section 114 notice, shows severe expenditure control problems.
findings.figures: £2.2 million additional overspend vs budget; £17.2 million reserves use (vs £15 million budgeted); £33.6 million EFS; £13.3 million services overspend
findings.quote: At Quarter 3 (December) 2025/26, the Council is forecasting an indicative breakeven position after use of £17.2 million of reserves (£2.2 million more than the budgeted £15 million due to overspends in Adult and Children's Services) and a further £33.6 million of Exceptional Financial Support.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: £194.1 million Special Educational Needs deficit is hidden from the balance sheet and crystallises when statutory override expires March 2028
findings.detail: The council holds approximately £194.1 million of accumulated unfunded SEND expenditure by March 2026, masked by a temporary statutory override that allows it to be excluded from accounts. This override expires March 2028. If government does not assume responsibility for funding SEND or approve a mechanism for addressing the legacy deficit by then, councils will be forced to recognise these liabilities. The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant (to pay 90% of deficits in Autumn 2026), but the mechanism for the remaining debt and a cumulative national deficit of approximately £14 billion remains unresolved.
findings.matters: This is a latent liability of exceptional size that will either require massive additional revenue funding, further borrowing capacity, or a Section 114 notice if not resolved by central government; it represents the council's single largest financial risk.
findings.figures: £194.1 million accumulated SEND deficit by March 2026; £14 billion cumulative national deficit by March 2028; any local borrowing solution estimated at £7.5 million annually in revenue costs
findings.quote: By March 2026, Worcestershire County Council is forecast to hold approximately £194.1 million of additional debt arising from unfunded expenditure on statutory Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) services over several years. This represents the Council's most significant financial risk.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Council cannot set a balanced budget without Exceptional Financial Support and council tax flexibility above referendum limits
findings.detail: The council faces a £59.933 million budget gap for 2026/27 after the Final Local Government Settlement. This is being bridged by approved council tax flexibility of 4% (worth £14.4 million per year) and a requested Capitalisation Direction as part of the EFS framework. The Section 151 Officer has made formal submissions to MHCLG requesting both.
findings.matters: A council unable to set a lawful budget without government-granted dispensations is a fundamental credit risk to any lender; the reliance on central government discretion removes financial autonomy.
findings.figures: £59.933 million budget gap; 4% council tax flexibility granted worth £14.4 million per year (£43.2 million over MTFP period); Capitalisation Direction requested
findings.quote: the Council's financial position is critical, given its inability since 2025/26 to set a balanced Revenue Budget without reliance upon Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital expenditure is forecast to increase 100% over five years (£97m in 2024/25 to £141.7m by 2028/29), placing sustained pressure on borrowing and MRP charges.
findings.detail: Table 3 shows capital expenditure increasing from £97.0m (2024/25 actual) to a peak of £193.8m (2026/27), then moderating to £141.7m (2028/29). The increase is driven by approved capital programmes but, combined with the DSG borrowing need, creates multiple years of elevated debt and MRP costs that will flow into revenue budgets for decades.
findings.matters: Sustained high capital expenditure locks the council into rising financing costs. MRP will become a larger revenue charge as the CFR grows. A lender needs to see that the council can sustain both the capital ambition and the resulting debt servicing obligations from within its operating budget.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2024/25: £97.0m; 2026/27 peak: £193.8m; net financing need 2026/27: £50.3m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Mercia Waste loan facility has been extended by 5 years with adjusted terms, and the council is exposed to refinancing risk when the extension ends in January 2029.
findings.detail: The council and Herefordshire jointly provided £92m (WCC's share, as at 31 March 2024) in financing for an Energy from Waste PFI with Mercia Waste. In 2024, they agreed to extend the contract by 5 years to January 2029 and reduce the bullet repayment amount from circa £128m to £106m, with Mercia paying the council £22m in principal on the extended Facility B. At the end of the extension in 2029, the facility must either be refinanced or the plant reverts to the councils.
findings.matters: The £92m loan is a material long-term asset, but the extension to 2029 creates a cliff refinancing risk in 2028-29 when other borrowing pressures may be acute. The council should clarify its plan for what happens when the extension ends.
findings.figures: Loan carrying value: £92m as at 31 March 2024; extended unitary payment reduction: £2.5m upfront, £4.5m p.a. (2022-23), £6m p.a. (2024 onwards); bullet repayment reduced to £106m; Mercia to pay £22m principal
findings.quote: In partnership with Herefordshire County Council, the County Council provided finance to Mercia Waste for the building of an Energy from Waste Plant, which they are operating for a period determined by the existing PFI contract... Loans granted to Mercia Waste for this purpose will be considered separately to normal Treasury Management investment activity... As at the 31 March 2024, the carrying value of the loan to Mercia Waste was £92m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Banking arrangements require the council to pay 4% over base rate on overdrafts while earning only base rate minus 75bp on deposits, creating a wide carry loss.
findings.detail: As of December 2025, the council's banking terms are: 4% over base rate on debit balances (overdraft), versus base rate minus 75 basis points on credit balances (deposits). With base rate at 4.00%, this means the council pays 8% on overdrafts while earning 3.25% on deposits. Given that the DSG position is forcing short-term borrowing, this spread is costly.
findings.matters: The 475bp spread between overdraft cost and deposit rate is wide and reflects weak negotiating position. With elevated debt levels, any reliance on overdraft facilities becomes expensive. A lender would want to see a renegotiation of these terms, particularly given the council's size.
findings.figures: Overdraft cost: base + 4% (= 8.00% at December 2025); deposit rate: base - 75bp (= 3.25% at December 2025); spread of 475bp
findings.quote: As at December 2025, Worcestershire County Council pays interest on the aggregate of the cleared debit balances at a rate of 4% over base rate and receives the base rate minus 75 basis points (BP) on the credit balance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement is forecast to grow 36% in four years (£731m to £997m), driven partly by £71.9m and £71m in assumed but unapproved Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: The council's CFR is forecast to climb from £731.0m (2024/25) to £996.6m (2027/28). Table 5 shows that £71.9m of the 2026/27 increase and £71.0m of the 2027/28 increase are assumed to come from EFS (capitalisation directions) that have not yet been approved by MHCLG. If EFS is not granted, actual borrowing needs would be lower but the council would face additional budget shortfalls.
findings.matters: The council is building multi-year budget projections on the assumption of unconfirmed government funding. If EFS is withheld or delayed, the council will face a shortfall requiring either further borrowing, service cuts, or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: CFR grows from £731.0m (2024/25) to £996.6m (2027/28); EFS assumed at £71.9m (2026/27) and £71.0m (2027/28), totalling £142.9m over two years
findings.quote: The County Council is asked to approve the following CFR projections as shown in Table 5. findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Including DSG, the council will be borrowing above its capital financing requirement (over-borrowed) from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.detail: Table 9 shows that excluding DSG, the council is properly under-borrowed with £130.2m headroom against its CFR. But including the DSG short-term borrowing, actual debt will exceed the CFR: 2026/27 debt of £964.7m against CFR of £873.7m, 2027/28 debt of £1,248.3m against CFR of £996.6m. This violates prudent borrowing principles because the borrowing is not matched to capital assets.
findings.matters: Over-borrowing against CFR indicates unsustainable debt levels and loss of control over borrowing ratios. A lender would be concerned that debt continues to grow after the government takes over DSG (2027/28 onwards debt forecast is still £1,225.3m).
findings.figures: Debt including DSG 2026/27: £964.7m vs CFR £873.7m; 2027/28: £1,248.3m vs CFR £996.6m; 2028/29: £1,225.3m (after DSG transfer, still elevated)
findings.quote: Borrowing above CFR (including DSG)? Yes [for 2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: DSG High Needs deficit is forcing unplanned short-term borrowing and eroding investment income by £7.5m annually until 2028.
findings.detail: The council lost £7.5m in treasury management income in 2025/26 due to DSG High Needs deficit cash flow. Additional short-term borrowing will continue until March 2028 when the government takes responsibility. The CFO notes the council would have met its balanced budget requirement 'if the Government funded SEND High Needs adequately', flagging this as a significant issue driven by government policy, not council overspend.
findings.matters: This represents forced borrowing outside the capital programme, reducing financial flexibility and increasing debt service costs. A lender would need to understand whether the council's deficit management plan survives once this £7.5m+ annual impact is removed.
findings.figures: £7.5m lost treasury income in 2025/26; expected short-term borrowing for DSG: £93.6m (2025/26), £127.6m (2026/27), £160.7m (2027/28)
findings.quote: This is a significant issue for the council due to the impact of cash flowing Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) High Needs which has costs us c£7.5 million in 2025/25 due to lost treasury management income.

findings.detail: The capital expenditure forecasts (Table 3) and CFR projections (Table 5) assume approval of Exceptional Financial Support totalling £143.9m over two years. This support is not yet in the approved capital programme; if not granted, the council would need to cut capital spend by nearly £72m each year or find alternative funding, directly reducing the projected CFR growth.

A lender should understand that if EFS is denied, the council's capital plans and borrowing need would shrink materially, or borrowing from other sources would be required to maintain the programme.
findings.figures: EFS included in CFR projections: £71.9m (2026/27) and £71.0m (2027/28); also noted in Table 5 as 'Assumed Net Financing Need for EFS not yet in Capital Programme'

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to grow from £731m to £997m over four years.

This growth is driven by capital programme spend of £150-194m per year plus Exceptional Financial Support grants of £71.9m (2026/27) and £71m (2027/28). This indebtedness must be serviced each year and repaid over asset lives.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 5 Worcestershire PF - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - updated for IAS19 distribution 260925
findings.headline: Investment valuations show £4.3 million timing differences that remain unadjusted in the financial statements
findings.detail: The auditors identified £4.318m of unadjusted differences between investment valuations in the Fund's financial statements and valuation statements from third-party investment managers. The differences arose because some Level 3 investment balances were valued using 31 December 2024 capital/NAV statements rather than 31 March 2025 statements, as the later statements were not available at the time the accounts were prepared. This was recorded as an unadjusted misstatement but deemed not material to the overall financial statements.
findings.matters: While marked immaterial, a £4.3m valuation gap indicates timing and coordination issues in obtaining investment valuations, and the cumulative unadjusted misstatements (including prior year £10.6m) total £14.996m across two years.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 5 Worcestershire PF - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - updated for IAS19 distribution 260925
findings.headline: Contributions are not reviewed and authorised before posting to the ledger, creating reliance on manual post-entry controls
findings.detail: The auditors identified that contributions received by the pension fund are not reviewed and authorised before being posted to the ledger. Instead, the fund relies on a formula-driven contribution monitoring spreadsheet as a compensating control. Management acknowledges this is a system limitation and plans to integrate review and authorisation controls within the new financial system (implementation timeline not specified).
findings.matters: Lack of pre-posting authorization represents a control weakness in transaction processing that increases risk of error or fraud entering the accounts. The effectiveness of the compensating manual control depends on consistent spreadsheet review.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: Contributions received are not reviewed and authorised before being posted to the ledger. However, the contribution monitoring spreadsheet is formula-driven highlights

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 5 Worcestershire PF - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - updated for IAS19 distribution 260925
findings.headline: Virgin Media pension scheme ruling creates unquantified contingent liability for LGPS funds including Worcestershire
findings.detail: The High Court ruled in Virgin Media v NTL Pension Trustees that certain defined benefit pension scheme amendments were invalid without proper actuarial certification. The Court of Appeal upheld this in July 2024. HM Treasury and Government Actuaries Department are investigating whether similar certificates exist for LGPS amendments. Management has disclosed this as a contingent liability in the financial statements, but the impact is not yet quantifiable.
findings.matters: A material adverse ruling on LGPS scheme amendments could expose the fund to significant unfunded liabilities or restructuring costs, depending on the scope of certificates found to be deficient.
findings.figures: Impact not yet quantifiable; disclosed as contingent liability
findings.quote: As the impact of the ruling of the Virgin media case is not yet quantifiable, management has included a disclosure within the contingent liability note of the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: SEND service rated level 3 (widespread systemic failings) by Ofsted and CQC in April 2024 with two priority actions still outstanding
findings.detail: An Ofsted and CQC joint inspection of the council's SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) service in April 2024 resulted in a level 3 grading, reporting 'widespread and/or systemic failings'. Two priority actions were required of the local area partnership. The auditor made a key recommendation that the council work at pace with partners to deliver the SEND priority actions to the timescales required. This service is statutory, its costs are driving the DSG deficit crisis, and the systemic failings indicate control problems.
findings.matters: SEND is one of the council's largest budget pressures and the primary driver of its £184m DSG deficit projection. Systemic service failings increase the risk of escalating costs and potential regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: Level 3 Ofsted/CQC rating (April 2024). Sufficiency planning remodelled with £30.1m investment over 3 years.
findings.quote: An Ofsted and CQC inspection of SEND was carried out in April 2024 and published on 15 July 2024. It was a level 3 grading reporting "widespread and/ or systemic failings" in the SEND service.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Performance management collapsed with no Cabinet reporting of corporate performance in 2024/25 or up to July 2025
findings.detail: The auditor found no corporate performance reporting to Cabinet in 2024/25, despite making an improvement recommendation in the prior year that the council enhance its performance monitoring arrangements. The council lacks a golden thread between its Corporate Plan and service delivery, 15 KPIs were not reviewed for three years, and performance reporting was only published on the website for 2023/24 until June 2025. The auditor identified this as a significant weakness because without performance management underpinned by robust data, the council cannot understand what improvements are needed.
findings.matters: Performance management is critical to effective financial control. The absence of regular performance reporting to senior decision-makers undermines the council's ability to identify problems early and make informed decisions about resource allocation and efficiency improvements.
findings.figures: Zero Cabinet performance reporting in 2024/25 and up to July 2025. 15 KPIs not reviewed for three years.
findings.quote: In 2024/25 and up to July 2025 the Cabinet saw no performance reporting. The Council has an insufficiently developed performance management framework with no golden thread in place between the Corporate Plan and Directorate and Service Plans

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased by £96.8m in a single year from £399.8m to £496.6m
findings.detail: The council's long-term borrowing rose from £399.8m on 31 March 2024 to £496.6m by 31 March 2025. Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m over the same period. This rapid increase in debt reflects the council's dependence on borrowing to fund its operations and capital programme, which adds to debt servicing costs and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender must assess debt sustainability. The pace and scale of borrowing growth, combined with the council's structural deficits and reserve depletion, raises questions about the council's ability to service and repay this debt.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing increased from £399.8m to £496.6m (increase of £96.8m). Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m
findings.quote: The Council's long-term borrowing increased from £399.8m on 31 March 2024 to £496.6m by 31 March 2025. Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m over this period.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Overspend on 2024/25 budget of £6.2m was met from planned reserves after the council had not delivered £10.8m in cost reductions
findings.detail: The 2024/25 outturn showed a net overspend of £6.2m on a £433.4m budget after using £7.9m of planned reserves. This came after the council failed to deliver £10.8m in planned savings. The auditor notes that the Senior Leadership Team and Chief Officers were instructed to find alternative savings when gaps emerged, but 'these did not materialise and the overspend was met from risk reserves'. This reveals both operational control weakness and reliance on reserves to cover budget misses.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can hold its budget. Missing savings targets and absorbing overruns from reserves indicates control issues and reduces confidence in budget forecasting.
findings.figures: 2024/25 budget £433.35m (including £35m structural deficit), outturn overspend £6.2m, covered by £7.9m planned reserves
findings.quote: The Senior Leadership Team and Chief Officers were instructed in 2024/25 to find alternative, achievable savings proposals where there are current gaps in delivery. We note these did not materialise and the overspend was met from risk reserves.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council is dependent on Exceptional Financial Support of £33.6m for 2025/26 and has requested £43.6m more for 2026/27, subject to external assurance review
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget of £495.6m is supported by £15m of reserves and £33.6m from Exceptional Financial Support, which will be borrowed at an estimated cost of £15m and is subject to external assurance review later in 2025. The council has also requested £43.6m in EFS to support 2026/27 budget setting, which is yet to be agreed. This indicates structural financial dependency on government emergency support that cannot continue indefinitely.
findings.matters: A lender must assess the sustainability of EFS dependence. These are exceptional measures with conditions attached, and the government may not extend support indefinitely. The council needs to demonstrate a path to financial independence.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budget £495.6m; EFS £33.6m (2025/26), £43.6m requested (2026/27); borrowing cost of EFS estimated at £15m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 net budget is £495.6m for 2025/26 supported by £15m of the risk reserves and £33.6m from Exceptional Financial Support (EFS). The Council also requested £43.6m to support 2026/27 budget setting.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Savings programme is delivering only 72% of target with a budget gap of £48.6m filled by reserves and emergency government support
findings.detail: In 2024/25, the council set a savings target of £37.2m but delivered only £27.6m (72%), leaving £10.8m undelivered including £4.69m in corporate savings. For 2025/26, the council included only £12.51m of savings proposals to address a budget gap of £48.6m. The remaining gap is filled by £15m from reserves and £33.6m from Exceptional Financial Support. The auditor made a key recommendation that savings must address the gap at scale and pace.
findings.matters: The council is not delivering the operational efficiencies needed to stabilise its finances. Heavy reliance on one-off reserves and government bailout funding rather than sustainable savings is not a viable long-term position for a lender to support.
findings.figures: 2024/25 savings target £37.2m, delivered £27.6m (72%). 2025/26 budget gap £48.6m, addressed with £12.51m savings plus £15m reserves and £33.6m EFS
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the Council had a savings target of £37.2m and it delivered £27.6m (72%). Of the £10.8m undelivered savings £4.69m were corporate savings from areas such as the management review... The Council is not identifying and delivering savings in line with the scale of its budget requirements.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Earmarked risk reserves falling from £43.5m to £7.1m by March 2026 as the council uses them to fund services
findings.detail: The council's four main earmarked risk reserves had an opening balance of £43.5m on 1 April 2024, fell to £28.7m in 2024/25, and are expected to reach only £7.1m by 31 March 2026. The council has already committed £15m of these reserves to balance the 2025/26 budget and £1.875m for a County Hall decommissioning options appraisal. This continued draw on reserves to support service provision is described as unsustainable.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's financial buffer is collapsing. Reserves at this level offer minimal protection against unexpected shocks or service pressures.
findings.figures: Opening balance £43.5m (1 April 2024), reducing to £28.7m (31 March 2025), expected to be £7.1m (31 March 2026)
findings.quote: The Council also has four main earmarked reserves held for risk, with a total opening balance of £43.5m on 1 April 2024 which reduced to £28.7m in 2024/25. The value of these reserves is expected to be £7.1m on 31 March 2026 which is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has doubled in a year and will exceed £184m by March 2026 with no reserves to cover it after the statutory override ends in 2028
findings.detail: The DSG deficit jumped from £44.2m on 31 March 2024 to £98.2m on 31 March 2025 (87% increase) and is projected at £184.4m by 31 March 2026. The council has no reserves to accommodate this deficit if the statutory override is lifted on 31 March 2028. The auditor identified a significant weakness and issued a statutory recommendation requiring the council to urgently develop and agree a deficit management plan to begin reducing the deficit over time.
findings.matters: This is a structural solvency risk. If the override is not extended, the council becomes liable for a deficit roughly equivalent to its entire general fund balance and earmarked reserves combined, threatening financial sustainability.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £44.2m (31 March 2024), £98.2m (31 March 2025), projected £184.4m (31 March 2026). Council has no reserves to cover this.
findings.quote: The Council has no reserves to accommodate this deficit if the statutory override is lifted on 31 March 2028 this is a significant risk to its financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £50m in the first half year reduces 2025/26 spend from £209m to £159m, signalling either planning delays or financing constraints
findings.detail: The original 2025/26 capital budget approved in February was £209m. By Month 6, this has been reprofiled down to £159m (£125m excluding EFS funding), a recashflow of £50m. Major delayed schemes include: A38 Bromsgrove Phases 2-6 (£10.7m), Bromsgrove High 2FE expansion (£4.7m), Hampton Bridge (£4.5m), Bus Services Improvement Grant (£3m), Expansion to increase Special School Capacity (£3m). The report notes capital managers must prioritise 'early reporting of slippage'.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage suggests either: (a) the council cannot finance its own borrowing at the pace planned, or (b) projects are poorly scoped and delayed. Either is a red flag. The combination with revenue overspends suggests a council struggling to execute its strategy.
findings.figures: £50m recashflowed from 2025/26 to later years, 2025/26 budget fell from £209m to £159m (24% reduction), actuals YTD £39m (31% of revised £125m non-EFS budget)
findings.quote: By the end of Quarter 2, £50 million of forecast spend has been recashflowed from 2025/26 to subsequent years, with the most significant areas of re-cashflow being: A38 Bromsgrove Phases 2 to 6: £10.7 million, Bromsgrove High 2FE expansion: £4.7 million, Hampton Bridge: £4.5 million

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Government has delayed SEND reforms from autumn 2025 to 2026, leaving the DSG funding crisis unaddressed for at least another year
findings.detail: The government was expected to set out SEND reform approaches in a Schools White Paper in autumn 2025, but has now delayed this to 2026. The council explicitly states this is 'massively disappointing' because 'We need comprehensive changes that will make the system sustainable and address the dramatic rise in costs we have seen over the last decade.' Without reforms, the £193.7m DSG deficit this year will continue to mount unchecked. The council notes that 38 county and largest unitary authorities in England have accumulated 'unmanageable' SEND deficits.
findings.matters: The structural SEND funding crisis is not being addressed by central government. Every quarter the deficit grows with no policy solution in sight. This removes any hope of the council 'growing into' the problem.
findings.figures: EHCP spending in England forecast to reach £21bn by 2029 (double the 2016 level), one-in-twenty pupils under 16 now have EHCP (up from 2.7% a decade ago)
findings.quote: The recent announcement from Government on the delay setting out reforms to special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) services until 'early' in 2026 is massively disappointing. We need comprehensive changes that will make the system sustainable and address the dramatic rise in costs we have seen over the last decade.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Revenue debt has grown to £41m with £6.6m in legal proceedings or litigation, indicating collection difficulties
findings.detail: Total council revenue debt at Period 6 is £41m, up from £37.7m in the same period last year (an increase of £3.3m or 8.7%). Of this, £6.6m is currently with Legal Services for review or in litigation. The report flags 'Debt recovery remains a key issue for the council' and the position is reported to members through Audit & Governance Committee.
findings.matters: Growing uncollectable debt signals either rising resident inability to pay (sign of local economic distress) or council ineffectiveness in recovery. £6.6m in litigation suggests disputes rather than straightforward arrears, which is harder to resolve.
findings.figures: £41m total revenue debt (up from £37.7m prior year same period, +£3.3m), £6.6m in legal review/litigation
findings.quote: Total council's revenue debt for Period 6 stands at £41 million. This is an increase when compared to the same period in 2024/25 when it was £37.7 million. Debt recovery remains a key issue for the council, with c£6.6 million of debt currently with Legal Services for review, or in litigation.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: The council is dependent on £33.6m of Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2025/26 and will need to request continuation for 2026/27 with a forecast gap of £63.7m
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget could not be balanced without £33.6m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), a Capitalisation Direction from Government under the Local Government Act 2003. At Month 6, this remains in place as government support 'in principle'. For 2026/27, the estimated budget gap is £63.7m. The report states 'we expect to update Cabinet again in December, ahead of bringing forward final proposals for the 2026/27 budget' and flags that 'Even assuming a request is granted for a continuation of Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 and Council Tax increases, the Council will have to find significant further savings in 2026/27 from reducing spending and/or increasing income to avoid a S114 Notice.'
findings.matters: EFS is a temporary bridge, not a structural fix. The fact that it is already needed for 2026/27 and the gap is rising signals the council cannot find its own way to balance without either finding £63m+ in savings or requesting emergency support indefinitely.
findings.figures: £33.6m EFS in 2025/26 budget, £63.7m estimated gap for 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget could not be balanced without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £33.6 million. Even assuming a request is granted for a continuation of Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 and Council Tax increases, the Council will have to find significant further savings in 2026/27 from reducing spending and/or increasing income to avoid a S114 Notice.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Only 88% of the £12.5m savings programme is on track; £0.3m is rated red and unachievable this year including the Vale Lodge £763k saving
findings.detail: The council approved £12.5m in savings for 2025/26. As at Month 6, 88% (£11.1m) is rated green, of which 81% (£10.1m) has been achieved. However, 9% (£1.1m) is amber and 2% (£0.3m) is red. The red savings are in Children's Services: Vale Lodge review £763k (delayed pending Cabinet decision), Fostering Respite £127k, Expansion of Internal Supported Living £151k, Positive Outcomes Project review £30k. Directors are expected to identify alternative savings to mitigate non-delivery.
findings.matters: If 12% of planned savings slip, the overspend widens and the council needs larger reserve drawdowns or deeper cuts. The red-rated Vale Lodge saving suggests operational decisions are stalled, not just delayed.
findings.figures: £12.5m total savings target, 88% green (£11.1m), 81% achieved (£10.1m), 9% amber (£1.1m), 2% red (£0.3m). Vale Lodge £763k unachievable this year.
findings.quote: 88% currently rated green (£11.1 million) of which 81% (£10.1 million) has been achieved to date, 9% amber (£1.1 million) and 2% red (£0.3 million)

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Usable reserves are collapsing, falling from £93.7m (March 2025) to a forecast £72.5m (March 2026), with only £19.6m of that being genuinely unrestricted risk reserves
findings.detail: Opening Earmarked Reserves were £93.7m. The council expects to draw down £21.2m this year, leaving £72.5m. However, of that closing balance, only £19.6m is classified as usable 'unearmarked' risk reserve (Finance Risk Reserve, Business Rates Retention, Transformation Reserve). The remainder is either ring-fenced to grants/health, schools, insurance, or commitments. The General Fund Balance is £19.2m (4.4% of budget) but the Section 151 Officer states it should be minimum 5% (£21.7m). The council is currently using £11.3m of reserves just to balance 2025/26. External Auditors have given a Key Recommendation to agree a reserves replenishment plan.
findings.matters: A council with £19.6m of liquid reserves to handle emergencies or service shocks is dangerously exposed. The target 5% buffer is considered minimum; Worcestershire is below it and falling. This severely constrains the council's ability to manage any adverse variance or demand spike.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £93.7m, closing forecast £72.5m, usable risk reserves only £19.6m (down from £28.7m March 2025), General Fund Balance £19.2m (4.4% of budget vs 5% target of £21.7m), £11.3m reserves drawn in 2025/26
findings.quote: The value of the Council's Earmarked reserves was £93.7 million, however this includes several ring-fenced grant related reserves. A total of £21.2 million of reserves are expected to be drawn down this year, leaving a forecast closing balance of £72.5 million. Of the £72.5 million forecast to be remaining at the year end, only c£19.6 million is deemed to be usable and unearmarked.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs deficit will rise from £98.2m to £193.7m in one year and will crystallize as a budget hit when the statutory override expires in March 2028
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs deficit opened at £98.2m (March 2025) and is forecast to reach £193.7m by year-end. The number of children with EHCPs has increased 2.75% in Q2 alone (to 7,806) and is up 20% year-on-year from 6,530. The statutory override allowing DSG deficits to sit off the main balance sheet expires March 2028. At that point, the forecast deficit will be approximately £322.2m and will hit the council's main revenue budget unless government provides additional funding. The External Auditor has issued a Statutory Recommendation on DSG management.
findings.matters: This is the single largest threat to Worcestershire's solvency. When the override expires, the council will either need to find £322m from reserves (which do not exist) or from additional cuts and savings that dwarf anything currently planned. Without reform to SEND funding, this is unavoidable.
findings.figures: Opening DSG deficit £98.2m (March 2025), forecast year-end £193.7m, forecast at March 2028 approximately £322.2m, EHCPs up 2.75% in Q2 to 7,806, up 20% year-on-year from 6,530
findings.quote: The accumulated deficit position for the DSG reserves at 1 April 2025 was a deficit balance of £98.2 million, built up from previous years overspends. Considering the current forecast for 2025/26, the deficit balance is expected to increase to £193.7 million at year-end

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Looked After Children external placements have risen 7% in a year with unit costs jumping 7-12%, driving an £8.1m overspend
findings.detail: External LAC placements are now 671 (September 2025) versus 651 in September 2024, a 7% annual increase. Agency Residential placements rose from 162 to 169 (+7 children) while unit cost jumped from £6,563/week to £7,123/week (+8.5%). Independent Fostering placements up 8 to 360 with unit cost rising from £1,000 to £1,055/week (+5.5%). Forecast overspend in Children's Services is £8.1m on a net budget of £107.3m.
findings.matters: Rising external LAC placements are sticky and expensive; the council is moving toward more costly residential care and cannot control unit prices set by private providers. This is symptomatic of a unable-to-manage social care system, not a temporary fluctuation.
findings.figures: External placements 671 (+20 in year = 7% increase), Agency Residential unit cost £6,563→£7,123/week, Independent Fostering £1,000→£1,055/week, 4% total LAC growth (1,035→1,071), forecast overspend £8.1m on £107.3m
findings.quote: the current demographic pressures in placements for Looked After Children and high inflation in care placements, which is a volatile area of forecasting. This is despite the recurrent budget being amended and growth and contract inflation being applied in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement demand is rising faster than any prior year, with unit costs inflating 6-16% above budget
findings.detail: Since March 2025, Adult Services have taken on 165 net new care packages (2.3% growth) versus 0.4% in the same period last year. Unit costs are rising well above inflation: Physical Disability Residential +12% (£157/person/week), Learning Disability Residential +6.7% (£149/person/week), Mental Health Residential +6.7% (£84/person/week). The service forecasts a £10.2m overspend on placements before mitigation, with total Adult Services overspend at £8.3m against a net budget of £173.9m.
findings.matters: Demand-driven cost pressures in social care are a leading indicator of a council losing control of its largest budget area. Placement cost inflation above general CPI signals either market stress or the council accepting unprofitable contracts. This is recurring, not one-off.
findings.figures: 165 net new packages (2.3% six-month growth vs 0.4% prior year), unit costs +12% in Physical Disability Residential, +6.7% Learning Disability, +6.7% Mental Health, forecast overspend £8.3m on £173.9m budget
findings.quote: For the past four financial years placement activity and the unit cost of providing care has been higher than forecast despite the recurrent budget being amended and significant growth and contract inflation being applied to the budget. Demand has continued to rise in the first half year of 2025/26 and at a higher pace than the same period in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: The council is at risk of issuing a Section 114 notice and needs to avoid it by continuous focus on financial management
findings.detail: The Council explicitly confirms in its recommendations that it 'needs to continue to demonstrate its commitment to avoid the need to issue a Section 114 notice in 2025/26'. A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that the council faces insolvency. The Section 25 Statement already highlighted risks of needing one given the MTFP forecast and reducing reserves, though a programme of activities has commenced.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice would trigger severe restrictions on spending and governance, making the council unmortgageable and signalling imminent service collapse to lenders and investors.
findings.figures: £33.6m Exceptional Financial Support required just to balance 2025/26; £63.7m estimated gap for 2026/27
findings.quote: confirms that the whole Council needs to continue to demonstrate its commitment to avoid the need to issue a Section 114 notice in 2025/26 by continuous focus of financial management actions to reduce the forecast overspend

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Reform party took minority administration in May 2025 with 27 of 57 councillors, and council is developing a Local Government Reorganisation Business Case with November 2025 timescale.
findings.detail: Worcestershire held elections in May 2025. Reform secured a minority administration with 27 elected councillors. The council is 'currently developing the Local Government Reorganisation Business Case for the November 2025 timescale.' LGR (merger with Herefordshire) is a significant structural change. A minority administration during a period of severe budget pressure and an LGR process creates governance uncertainty. The recovery plan the council needs to deliver may be overtaken by LGR.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change whose terms, cost, and staffing implications are unknown. It could distract from the urgent deficit and DSG recovery work, or alternatively could provide a reset opportunity. Lenders need clarity on whether the council's recovery plan is independent of LGR assumptions.
findings.figures: Reform secured minority administration: 27 of 57 councillors (May 2025). LGR Business Case due November 2025.
findings.quote: The Council is currently developing the Local Government Reorganisation Business Case for the November 2025 timescale. The most recent elections were in May 2025 when Reform secured a minority administration with 27 elected councillors.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: No performance reporting to Cabinet in 2024/25 — performance management framework is insufficiently developed with no 'golden thread' to corporate plan.
findings.detail: The auditor found that 'In 2024/25 and up to July 2025 the Cabinet saw no performance reporting.' The council lacks 'a golden thread in place between the Corporate Plan and Directorate and Service Plans, Financial plans' and 'performance, risk and financial planning are not aligned.' The auditor raised key recommendation KR3 requiring the council to 'significantly improve performance management' and align reporting. This represents a governance failure — the council cannot demonstrate that it is executing its strategy or that services are improving.
findings.matters: If a council's leadership is not seeing performance data, they cannot make informed decisions about where to cut. This is the governance failure underlying the savings shortfalls and budget overruns.
findings.figures: No performance reporting to Cabinet in 2024/25. 15 KPIs were not reviewed for three years.
